title: PAUL SAID, “I CAN DO ALL THINGS”—BUT NOBODY TALKS ABOUT WHAT HE WAS SUFFERING WHEN HE SAID IT.
paragraphs: PAUL SAID, “I CAN DO ALL THINGS”—BUT NOBODY TALKS ABOUT WHAT HE WAS SUFFERING WHEN HE SAID IT.

Before you quote Philippians 4:13 over your next victory, you need to understand the hunger, humiliation, uncertainty, and suffering behind those words. Because Paul wasn't promising that Jesus would give him everything he wanted. He was revealing something far more powerful: Jesus would be enough even when life gave him almost nothing.
There is something heartbreaking about the way we have learned to quote one of the most famous verses in the Bible.
We put it on shirts.
We print it on coffee mugs.
We write it beneath graduation pictures, business announcements, gym selfies, and photographs celebrating our greatest accomplishments.
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.” — Philippians 4:13 (KJV)
Beautiful words.
Powerful words.
Absolutely true words.
But what if I told you that the man who wrote them wasn't celebrating a promotion?
He wasn't standing on a stage holding a trophy.
He wasn't announcing that his financial problems had finally disappeared.
He wasn't telling the world that every prayer had been answered exactly the way he wanted.
He was a prisoner.
And before he wrote about doing all things through Christ, he wrote about knowing what it meant to be hungry.
To have little.
To suffer need.
To live without the comforts people often mistake for evidence of God's favor.
Read that again.
The man who declared that Christ strengthened him was also a man who knew what it felt like to go without.
And perhaps the reason this verse has become so familiar yet so misunderstood is that we love the promise of strength, but we rarely want to talk about the suffering that revealed it.
Because there is a version of Christianity that celebrates Jesus when the bills are paid, the family is healthy, the business is growing, and the prayers seem to be working.
But what happens when the bills are still unpaid?
When the diagnosis doesn't change?
When the marriage is still struggling?
When the person you prayed for still walks away?
When you have believed, obeyed, given, served, forgiven, and waited—and somehow your circumstances have become harder instead of easier?
Can you still say, “I can do all things through Christ”?
Paul could.
But not for the reason many people think.
And the truth behind his words may completely change the way you understand your own suffering.

Paul's letter to the Philippians was written while he was imprisoned. The precise location of that imprisonment is debated among scholars, with Rome traditionally identified and other locations proposed. But the central reality is unmistakable: Paul wrote while facing confinement, uncertainty, and the possibility of death.
He was not writing from a position of worldly security.
He was writing as a man whose circumstances could have given him every human reason to despair.
Yet listen carefully to what he said immediately before the famous verse.
“I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.” — Philippians 4:12 (KJV)
Did you catch that?
“To be hungry.”
“To suffer need.”
Those words are not decorative.
They are the context.
Paul wasn't claiming that faith had exempted him from hardship.
He was explaining how Christ sustained him through hardship.
He knew what it meant to have enough food.
And he knew what it meant not to have enough.
He knew seasons of provision.
And he knew seasons of deprivation.
He had experienced abundance.
And he had endured need.
Yet he had discovered something that neither prosperity nor poverty could teach him by itself.
His strength was not found in having everything.
His strength was found in belonging to Someone who would never abandon him.
Now look at the original Greek.
Philippians 4:13 reads:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με.
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.
A close translation is:
“I have strength for all things in the One who strengthens me.”
The Greek word ἰσχύω (ischyō) expresses having strength or being able.
The participle ἐνδυναμοῦντί (endynamounti) comes from a verb meaning to strengthen or empower.
And πάντα (panta) means “all things.”
But here is where context matters.
“All things” does not mean Paul could accomplish absolutely anything he imagined.
It refers to the circumstances he had just described.
Having plenty.
Having little.
Being full.
Being hungry.
Living in abundance.
Suffering need.
Paul was saying that through the strength supplied by Christ, he could endure and remain faithful in every one of those circumstances.

The Greek text does not explicitly include the name “Christ” in the final phrase, although many manuscript traditions and translations do. In the shorter reading reflected in several modern critical editions, the phrase says “the One who strengthens me.” The wider context of Philippians makes Paul's dependence upon Christ clear.
And that distinction matters because biblical confidence should rest on what Scripture actually teaches, not on words we wish it had said.
Paul's declaration was not a blank check for personal ambition.
It was a testimony of Christ-sustained endurance.
And there is an enormous difference between those two things.
One says, “Because I believe in Jesus, I will never lose.”
The other says, “Even when I lose what this world considers important, Jesus will remain my strength.”
One makes circumstances the measure of victory.
The other makes faithfulness to Christ the measure of endurance.
One falls apart when life doesn't cooperate.
The other can weep, suffer, struggle, and still cling to the Savior.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction desperately.
Because perhaps you have been quietly wondering whether your suffering means you have failed God.
You see other Christians celebrating breakthroughs while you are still trying to survive.
Someone posts about buying a house.
You are wondering how to pay the rent.
Someone shares a testimony about miraculous healing.
You are sitting beside a hospital bed, praying through another frightening night.
Someone announces that God has opened an extraordinary door.
You have been knocking on the same closed door for years.
And somewhere inside your exhausted heart, a question begins to form.
Lord, what am I doing wrong?
You have prayed.
You have tried to obey.
You have repented when convicted.
You have asked for wisdom.
You have held on when letting go seemed easier.
Yet your situation remains painful.
So you begin wondering whether your faith is too small.
Whether God is disappointed.
Whether the promises you have heard preached were somehow meant for everyone except you.
But listen.
Paul's hunger was not proof that Christ had abandoned him.
His imprisonment was not proof that the Gospel had failed.
His hardship was not proof that his obedience had been meaningless.
And your suffering, by itself, is not proof that God has rejected you.
That is not an excuse to ignore sin, refuse repentance, or avoid responsibility.
It is a reminder that suffering and divine abandonment are not the same thing.
Sometimes hardship comes through our own foolish choices.
Sometimes it comes through the sins of others.
Sometimes it comes through sickness, injustice, loss, or the brokenness of a fallen world.
And sometimes we do not know why a particular trial has been permitted.
Scripture does not give us permission to assign a simple spiritual explanation to every painful circumstance.
But it does give us permission to trust the character of God when we cannot understand His providence.
And Paul knew that truth personally.
Remember who he was before he became the apostle whose letters would strengthen generations of believers.
He was Saul.
A persecutor of the church.
A man who approved of Stephen's death and pursued Christians with frightening determination.
He believed he was serving God while opposing the people who belonged to Jesus.
Then, on the road to Damascus, everything changed.
The risen Christ confronted him.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” — Acts 9:4 (KJV)
Imagine that moment.
The man who thought he was defending God's honor discovered that he was persecuting God's Messiah.
His religious confidence collapsed.
His self-righteousness was exposed.
His entire understanding of himself was shattered.
But Jesus did not confront Saul merely to leave him in condemnation.
The Lord called him into a radically different life.
The persecutor would become a preacher.
The enemy of the church would become its servant.
The man who had contributed to the suffering of believers would himself suffer for the name of Christ.
And here is the part that should make every struggling Christian stop and think.
When Jesus called Paul, He did not promise him a comfortable life.
In Acts 9:16, the Lord said:
“For I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake.” (KJV)
Not how wealthy he would become.
Not how admired he would be.
Not how effortlessly his ministry would grow.
How great things he must suffer.
And still, Paul followed Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not fundamentally about Jesus making our earthly lives easier.
It is about Jesus reconciling sinners to God through His death and resurrection, forgiving the guilty, giving new life, and transforming those who belong to Him.
It is about a Savior worth following even when following Him costs us something.
That is why Paul's testimony carries such extraordinary weight.
He wasn't speaking about suffering from a safe distance.
He had lived it.
In 2 Corinthians 11:23–27, Paul described imprisonments, beatings, dangers, sleepless nights, hunger, thirst, cold, and exposure.
He had endured physical pain.
He had faced opposition.
He had experienced exhaustion.
He had known the vulnerability of having insufficient food and inadequate protection.
And yet the same man could write:
How?
Because he had learned a secret that many of us spend our entire lives trying to avoid learning.
Christ can be sufficient even when circumstances remain insufficient.
That does not mean hunger is good.
It does not mean poverty should be romanticized.
It does not mean injustice should be tolerated or that struggling people should be denied practical help.
In fact, the very passage containing Philippians 4:13 is part of Paul's heartfelt response to the Philippian believers who had supported him materially.
Their generosity mattered.
Their partnership mattered.
Their willingness to help someone in need mattered.
Paul was not teaching believers to ignore suffering.
He was showing them that their deepest security rested in Christ while also expressing gratitude for the people God used to meet his needs.
And perhaps that is another truth we have overlooked.
Sometimes the answer to someone's prayer for provision comes through the obedience and generosity of another believer.
Sometimes the person who says, “God will provide,” is also being called to become part of that provision.
Because Christian love is not merely a feeling we express.
It is something we practice.
But there is an even deeper truth hiding in Paul's words.
Go back one verse earlier.
Philippians 4:11 says:
“Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.” (KJV)
Notice the word.
Learned.
Paul did not say contentment came naturally.
He did not say he had never struggled.
He did not say he was born with extraordinary emotional resilience.
He said he had learned.
The Greek word translated “content” is αὐτάρκης (autarkēs), a term associated with being sufficient or content with one's circumstances.
In some Greek philosophical settings, the term was connected with self-sufficiency.
But Paul's explanation moves in a profoundly Christ-centered direction.
His contentment was not rooted in the idea that he needed nobody.
His confidence rested in the One who strengthened him.
He was not celebrating independence from God.
He was testifying to dependence upon God.
And that means contentment is not the absence of desire.
It is not pretending that pain doesn't hurt.
It is not denying that hunger is uncomfortable or that grief is devastating.
It is learning that our relationship with Christ is not destroyed when our circumstances change.
You can desire healing and still trust Jesus.
You can pray for provision and still remain faithful while waiting.
You can grieve a loss and still believe in the resurrection.
You can acknowledge your weakness without surrendering your hope.
Contentment is not emotional numbness.
It is a growing confidence that Christ remains worthy and faithful in every season.
And sometimes that lesson is learned through tears.
Not because tears make someone less spiritual.
But because faith does not require pretending to be unaffected by suffering.
Even Jesus wept.
Even Jesus experienced sorrow.
In Gethsemane, facing the suffering before Him, Jesus prayed:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42 (KJV)
Think about that.
Our Savior did not teach surrender from a place of comfortable detachment.
He entered the depths of human suffering without sin.
He was betrayed.
He was rejected.
He was mocked.
He was beaten.
He was crucified.
And at the cross, the One who had committed no sin bore our sins.
The Gospel does not invite us to trust a Savior who knows nothing about suffering.
It invites us to trust the crucified and risen Lord.
The One who suffered for our redemption.
The One whom death could not hold.
The One who now intercedes for His people.
And this is where Paul's words become more than an inspirational quotation.
They become a window into the power of the Gospel.
Because the greatest example of divine strength was not a man achieving everything he wanted.
It was Jesus Christ accomplishing the Father's saving purpose through suffering, obedient even unto death, and rising victorious over the grave.
The cross looked like defeat to those who did not understand what God was accomplishing.
But through that cross, Christ secured redemption for sinners.
And the resurrection declared that death would not have the final word.
That is why Christian hope is not dependent on every earthly situation improving immediately.
Our hope rests on a living Savior.
A Savior who can sustain us now.
A Savior who promises resurrection life.
A Savior whose grace reaches further than our worst failures.
A Savior whose faithfulness is greater than our changing circumstances.
And perhaps you need to hear something else.
Paul did not always experience the removal of his suffering.
In 2 Corinthians 12, he described a painful affliction he called a thorn in the flesh.
He pleaded with the Lord three times for it to depart.
But the Lord's answer was not the removal Paul requested.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)
There it is again.
Strength.
Not the strength of pretending.
Not the strength of never crying.
Not the strength of having everything under control.
The strength of Christ meeting a weak and dependent servant with sufficient grace.
And Paul responded:
“Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)
Do you see the connection?
Philippians 4:13 does not stand alone.
It belongs to the same Gospel-shaped understanding of weakness, grace, dependence, and perseverance that runs through Paul's letters.
The strength Paul celebrated was not self-exaltation.
It was Christ's power sustaining him.
And that changes everything.
Because some of us have been measuring spiritual maturity by how invincible we appear.
We hide our tears.
We conceal our struggles.
We pretend the family is fine.
We smile at church while carrying burdens nobody knows about.
We say, “God is good,” which is true, but sometimes we use those words to avoid admitting that we are hurting.
We are terrified that if someone sees our weakness, they will question our faith.
But Paul did not build his testimony around appearing untouchable.
He openly acknowledged weakness.
He openly described hardship.
He openly admitted suffering.
And then he pointed to Christ.
Maybe the testimony you have been afraid to share is the very testimony another believer needs to hear.
Not because your pain is the center of the story.
But because Jesus is worthy of praise even in the middle of it.
Maybe somebody needs to know that you still pray even when you feel exhausted.
That you still open your Bible even when you have questions.
That you still believe Jesus is Lord even when your heart is breaking.
That you have not always responded perfectly.
That there have been moments when fear overwhelmed you.
That you have needed forgiveness, correction, comfort, and help.
And that through it all, Christ has not ceased to be your Savior.
There is no shame in confessing that you need grace.
There is no spiritual prize for pretending to be stronger than you are.
The Christian life begins with admitting that we cannot save ourselves.
Why would we then pretend that we can sustain ourselves without Christ?
Maybe the most powerful words you can pray tonight are not, “Lord, make me successful.”
Maybe they are:
“Lord, teach me to remain faithful.”
“Teach me to trust You when I cannot see what You are doing.”
“Forgive me for treating Your blessings as proof that You love me more.”
“Forgive me for doubting Your love whenever life becomes difficult.”
“Help me to receive provision with gratitude and endure hardship without abandoning You.”
“Give me wisdom to act where I can act, humility to accept help where I need help, and courage to obey You whatever tomorrow brings.”
“Jesus, be my strength.”
You can simply write “Christ, strengthen me.”
Not as a formula that guarantees a breakthrough.
Not as a public performance of faith.
But as a sincere prayer from someone who knows they cannot walk this road alone.
There is something beautiful about believers refusing to let one another suffer in silence.
Not everyone needs to know the details of your battle.
But you were never meant to carry every burden without the love and prayers of the body of Christ.
And please remember this.
Philippians 4:13 is not telling you that you can do whatever you want.
It is reminding you that Christ can strengthen you to face what faithfulness requires.
It does not guarantee that every business will succeed.
It does not guarantee that every relationship will be restored.
It does not guarantee that every illness will be healed in this life.
It does not guarantee wealth, fame, influence, or uninterrupted comfort.
But it gives believers something more enduring than a promise of worldly success.
It points them to the sufficiency of Christ.
And that truth can sustain someone sitting in a hospital room.
Someone starting over after losing a job.
Someone grieving a loved one.
Someone battling temptation and learning to repent.
Someone seeking reconciliation after causing terrible harm.
Someone trying to rebuild a life damaged by sinful choices.
Someone who once walked far from God and is now learning what it means to come home through Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not merely good news for people whose lives look impressive.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
For the guilty who need forgiveness.
For the broken who need restoration.
For the proud who need humility.
For the weary who need strength.
For the lost who need reconciliation with God.
Paul himself was living proof.
His past was stained by persecution.
His present was marked by suffering.
But his identity was no longer defined by his former sins or his present chains.
He belonged to Jesus Christ.
And that is the heartbeat of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus erases the historical reality of what we have done.
Not because following Him eliminates every consequence.
Not because salvation promises a painless life.
But because through His death and resurrection, Jesus forgives repentant sinners, reconciles them to God, and begins transforming lives that sin once ruled.
Paul's past did not make him beyond the reach of mercy.
His chains did not place him beyond the reach of grace.
His hunger did not place him beyond the reach of Christ's strength.
And if you belong to Jesus, your present hardship cannot separate you from His love.
Romans 8:35 asks:
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (KJV)
Notice that word again.
Famine.
Paul knew that faithfulness to Jesus did not make believers immune to terrible circumstances.
But he also knew that terrible circumstances could not overturn the saving love of God in Christ.
This is not a promise that every earthly story will end the way we want.
It is a promise that those who belong to Christ have a hope stronger than death itself.
And that is why we must be careful not to turn Philippians 4:13 into a slogan for personal glory.
The purpose of Christian strength is not to make us look extraordinary.
It is to enable us to honor the Lord who sustains us.
If God gives you abundance, glorify Him with gratitude, generosity, and faithful stewardship.
If you are experiencing need, seek appropriate help, work wisely where you are able, receive the care of fellow believers, and continue trusting Christ.
If He opens a door, walk through it with humility.
If He calls you to wait, do not assume waiting means you have been forgotten.
If He corrects you, repent.
If you fall into sin, turn back to Him.
If you are weary, remember that strength is not something you must manufacture to earn His love.
The Savior who calls His people to follow Him is also the Savior who supplies grace for their journey.
And if this message has helped you see Philippians 4:13 differently, please do not let it end with you.
There is someone on your Facebook friends list who has been quietly questioning whether God still cares.
Someone who feels embarrassed because they cannot afford what others take for granted.
Someone who has mistaken hardship for divine rejection.
Someone who needs to hear that Paul's testimony was not built on comfort but on Christ.
Not merely to spread another inspirational post, but to help someone encounter Scripture in its context and discover the hope of the Gospel.
Because the next time life becomes difficult, you may need to remember that Philippians 4:13 was written by a man who knew both abundance and hunger.
We are not here to promise a life without suffering.
We are here to proclaim Jesus Christ.
His holiness.
His mercy.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His call to repentance.
His power to forgive, redeem, and transform.
Our desire is to make biblical encouragement, Christian learning, and spiritual nourishment accessible to people who are hungry to know Jesus more deeply.
And if this ministry has been strengthening your faith, I want to extend a personal invitation.
For those who choose to give in this way, that support can be an expression of Christian generosity and stewardship, offered to the glory of God.
The Bible calls believers to generosity, but it also teaches that giving should be willing rather than pressured.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Your responsibilities to your household, your local church, and those in genuine need matter.
Think of the believer who finds a devotional at the right moment.
The exhausted parent who reads a Gospel-centered article after everyone else has gone to sleep.
The struggling Christian who discovers that repentance is not the end of hope but the path back to fellowship with God.
But together, we can keep making biblical resources available, keep sharing Christ-centered teaching, and keep pointing people beyond temporary motivation toward the Savior Himself.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, conversation starters, or thoughtful gifts. But they are not the reason we exist.
Jesus is.
His Gospel is.
And helping people know Him more faithfully is the mission.
You do not have to pay to belong among people who are seeking to grow in Christ.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But faithful partnership can help us keep telling others about that gift.
And before you leave, I want to ask you one question.
Not about your income.
Not about your accomplishments.
Not about how successful your life looks from the outside.
But about your heart.
If God does not change your circumstances as quickly as you hoped, will you still trust the Savior who gave Himself for you?
You do not have to answer carelessly.
Paul did not learn contentment overnight.
He learned it through real circumstances.
And you may still be learning.
Perhaps your faith feels fragile.
Perhaps your prayers have become shorter.
Perhaps you are carrying disappointment that you have been afraid to admit.
Perhaps you have been using Philippians 4:13 as a promise that everything would eventually go your way.
And now you are realizing that its meaning is deeper.
It is not about having the power to control every outcome.
It is about depending on Christ through every circumstance.
So be honest.
Someone may need to know that faith can survive a season they never imagined enduring.
But please, do not stop at admiring Paul's faith.
Look to Paul's Savior.
Because the same apostle who said, “I can do all things,” also said:
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” — Philippians 1:21 (KJV)
That was the center of his life.
Not achievement.
Not applause.
Not wealth.
Not freedom from discomfort.
Christ.
Christ when he had plenty.
Christ when he had nothing.
Christ when people welcomed him.
Christ when people opposed him.
Christ when he was free.
Christ when he was imprisoned.
Christ when he was strong.
Christ when he was weak.
And when Paul spoke of contentment, he was not telling us that the world could never hurt him.
He was telling us that the world could never replace his Savior.
That is the testimony we need to recover.
Not a Christianity that only knows how to celebrate when everything is going well.
But a faith rooted so deeply in the crucified and risen Christ that even suffering cannot erase its hope.
One day, every believer in Christ will discover the fullness of what God has promised.
Not because every earthly dream came true.
But because the Savior who died and rose again will bring His redeemed people into the fullness of His presence.
Until then, we live by faith.
We pray.
We obey.
We repent.
We help one another.
We receive grace.
We endure.
And when our own strength fails, we remember where Paul found his.
Not in a prison door opening.
Not in a full stomach.
Not in the applause of the crowd.
But in Jesus Christ.
So the next time you read Philippians 4:13, remember the verse before it.
Remember the hunger.
Remember the need.
Remember the prison.
Remember the Savior.
And when you whisper, “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me,” do not hear a promise that you will never suffer.
Hear the testimony of a man who had suffered deeply and found Christ faithful.
Because the greatest miracle in Paul's prison was not that every chain had fallen off—it was that even while he was chained, his hope in Christ was still alive.
